opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to illustrate it is to start with the inputs rather than the outputs. If you look at the history of machine learning over the past ten or fifteen years, one of the most robust regularities we've seen is that the amount of compute used to train the largest models has been growing at a remarkably steady rate, something like four to five times per year. That trend has held up through a lot of changes in architectures, in which labs are leading, and in what the models are used for. So when people talk about extrapolating trends, the most defensible version is to say: if this kind of input growth continues for a few more years, what does that imply?

Then you connect those inputs to capabilities. We have scaling laws that tell us, fairly reliably, how a model's loss on its training objective improves as you add compute, data and parameters. The harder step is going from loss to things we actually care about, like whether a model can write working software, do a literature review, or carry out a long multi-step task on its own. There you can look at benchmarks over time and see how performance has moved as compute has scaled, and you can try to fit a curve to that.

A concrete example would be the length of tasks AI systems can complete autonomously. A few years ago models could only reliably do things that would take a human a few seconds or minutes. Now they can handle tasks that take a human much longer, and that horizon has been growing at a fairly consistent rate. If you take that rate and project it forward, you get a rough sense of when systems might handle tasks that take a person a day, a week, or a month. That's an extrapolation, and it says something quite substantive about the economic impact you might expect.

I'd add some caveats, though. Benchmarks saturate, they don't always measure what we think, and the relationship between benchmark performance and real-world usefulness is messy. There are also physical and economic constraints on inputs: power, chip manufacturing capacity, the cost of training runs, and the available supply of high-quality data. So I treat extrapolation as a baseline, not a prediction. You ask: what happens if the trend continues, and then what would have to be true for it to break? Often that second question is more informative, because it forces you to think about where the actual bottlenecks are.

r001.rationale: The candidate extrapolates compute growth and task-completion horizons, but does not describe a flat historical trajectory in AI mathematical capabilities as the basis for a prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I'd put it is that extrapolating trends in AI is really about asking: what are the inputs that have been driving progress, how fast have those inputs been growing, and how much longer can that growth continue?

So the most basic version is compute. If you look at the amount of compute used to train frontier models, it's been growing at something like four to five times per year for over a decade. That's an extraordinarily fast rate. If you just naively extend that line, you get to a point within a few years where training runs are consuming a meaningful fraction of global electricity production or chip manufacturing capacity. So the trend can't continue forever at that rate, and part of the exercise is figuring out where the bottlenecks start to bind.

But compute by itself doesn't tell you about capabilities. So the second layer is: how does compute translate into performance? Here you have things like scaling laws, which give you a fairly predictable relationship between compute, data, model size, and loss on the training objective. And then you have the harder question of how loss translates into things people actually care about, like whether a model can do a software engineering task or pass a benchmark. That second mapping is much noisier.

One way I like to illustrate it is with benchmarks like the ones that measure how long a task a model can complete autonomously. If you look at the horizon length of tasks that models can do, it's been doubling every several months. You can extrapolate that and say, okay, in a few years models should be doing tasks that take humans days or weeks. That's a legitimate extrapolation. But you also have to be honest that benchmarks tend to saturate, they often don't capture the messiness of real-world work, and the trend might bend as you move from well-specified problems to open-ended ones.

So I'd say the discipline is: identify the trend, understand the mechanism behind it, project it forward, and then ask carefully where the mechanism breaks down. The failure mode is either to draw a straight line and treat it as destiny, or to dismiss extrapolation altogether. Both are mistakes. Trends have been remarkably stable in this field, which is why extrapolation has worked well so far, but the reasons they've been stable are things like abundant capital and spare manufacturing capacity, and those don't last indefinitely.

r001.rationale: The response extrapolates compute growth and autonomous task horizons, but it does not describe a flat historical trajectory in AI mathematical capabilities or use one as the basis for a prediction.

astra-6.text:
One way to illustrate it is to imagine looking at AI progress a few years ago. You see that models tend to perform better as you increase the amount of compute used to train them, give them more data, and improve the algorithms. You can then ask: if those trends continue, what should we expect models to be able to do in another few years?

The tricky part is connecting a measurable trend to a capability you actually care about. Predicting that a model’s loss—a measure of how well it predicts text—will improve is one thing. Predicting when it will be able to do the work of a software engineer is much harder. You need some relationship between that underlying improvement and performance on real tasks.

So extrapolation is essentially taking a pattern we’ve observed and projecting it forward, conditional on the forces driving it continuing. It can be useful, but the further you go beyond what you’ve observed, the more uncertainty there is about whether the pattern will hold.

r001.rationale: The response describes projecting observed trends in compute, data, algorithms, and model performance, but it does not use an apparently flat historical trajectory in AI mathematical capabilities as the basis for a prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to illustrate it is to look at weather forecasting. Suppose you want to know how good weather forecasts will be ten years from now. You could try to anticipate every improvement in algorithms and computing hardware, but you could also look at how forecast accuracy has improved over time and project that trend forward.

You can do something similar with AI. You look at how performance on some task changes as models get more compute, more data, or better training methods. If you see a fairly consistent relationship, you can ask what would happen if those inputs continued to grow.

The important caveat is that you’re extrapolating a particular measurement. If a model’s score on a benchmark improves predictably, that doesn’t automatically tell you when it will be able to do an entire job. You still need to establish how the thing you’re measuring relates to the capability you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes projecting trends in weather forecasts and AI task performance, but it does not mention a historically flat trajectory in AI mathematical capabilities.
